extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patentees, and patent attorneys/draftspersons (practitioners drafting UK-style specifications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing a complete patent specification and claims so the invention is sufficiently and unambiguously disclosed, enabling a person skilled in the art to practise it and defining the scope of monopoly. Emphasis on avoidable defects (ambiguity, misdirection, improper claims) drawn from English case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: No essential feature left to experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: If some particular angle (feature) is essential, the specification must disclose it; leaving an essential element to be discovered by experiment makes the specification deficient and bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not omit or obscure any feature that is essential to make the invention work. If executing the invention requires discovering a particular parameter or part, specify it; do not require the public to find it by trial-and-error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty not to invite futile experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee, knowing that given materials will not answer the purpose, is bound so to word his specification as to prevent others from trying experiments on that which he knows will not answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you know certain alternatives will not work, you must not suggest them as suitable. Avoid broad or permissive language ('any suitable material') when you know only specific materials are effective; otherwise you mislead and may render the specification bad (example: paper heated by cloth claimed 'any suitable material' though only linen-wool worked).

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors obvious on face may be disregarded; experimental errors may vitiate
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors which a workman of ordinary skill and experience would perceive and correct on the face of the specification or drawings will not vitiate a patent; errors discoverable only by experiment and further inquiry may vitiate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typographical or self-evident mistakes that a skilled person would immediately correct are tolerable. But do not rely on the reader's experimental investigation to discover or correct an error — errors that require further experimentation to detect are dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: No false suggestion by asserting ineffective variants
rubrics_metrics.description: If a specification describes several processes or combinations and affirms they will produce a certain result, but some one of them is wholly ineffectual and useless, the patent will be bad even if the mistake would be obvious to an ordinary workman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving alternative methods or embodiments, ensure each described alternative is actually operative. Do not present non-working alternatives as equivalent options; doing so risks invalidation (Simpson v. Holliday).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement: intelligible to the skilled person without further invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be intelligible and enable the invention to be made without further invention by a person skilled in the particular kind of work; such a person may, however, require some trial or experiment when the subject is new or delicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write so that a person skilled in the art can produce the invention from the specification; allowance is made for reasonable trial/testing in new or delicate arts but not for additional inventive steps. Practical evidence that following the specification produces the article is strong proof of sufficiency (British Dynamite v. Krebs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Context of contemporary practice to be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: In construing a specification, the state of the particular manufacture at the date of the patent must be kept in view; where a skilled workman would know to perform or include certain customary operations (e.g., fitting a condenser), omission may be acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft with awareness of contemporary industry norms; some routine operations need not be spelled out if they are standard practice and would be understood by a skilled worker at the patent's date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text overrules erroneous drawings when error obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: If an attached drawing is erroneous so construction from it alone would fail, but the text correctly describes the construction or the error is one an ordinary workman would easily perceive and rectify (requiring regulation not experiments), the drawing error will be disregarded and will not vitiate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure text and drawings are consistent. If a drawing mistake would be obvious and correctable by a skilled reader, courts will often ignore it, but do not rely on this — correct drawings whenever possible (Otto v. Linford).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations: do not claim old parts as new
rubrics_metrics.description: When patenting a combination of well-known things, take care not to claim the old parts themselves as novel as well as the novel combination; if constituent parts are new and intended to be protected, they ought to be specially pointed out, fully described, and expressly claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only the combination is the invention, claims restricted to the combination suffice. If some constituent parts are themselves novel, describe and claim them separately if you wish protection for them. Avoid ambiguous drafting that might be read as claiming known parts as new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe and define the improvement in combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: In a patent for an improved arrangement or new combination, the specification must describe the improvement and define the novelty in a more specific form than a general description of the entire machine, so the improvement is ascertainable without minute comparisons with prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the improvement is the point of novelty (especially if small compared to the whole machine), point it out clearly and explain how it effects the improvement; do not bury it in a general description (Foxwell v. Bostock; Harrison v. Anderston Foundry Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: When claiming a combination only, separation of new/old parts not required
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only invention claimed is the combination and that is properly set forth, it is sufficiently described without separately distinguishing new parts from old; the combination itself constitutes the novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A properly limited combination claim will be valid even if the specification does not segregate which parts are old, provided the manner of arriving at and working the combination and its utility are sufficiently described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point out small improvements within large known machines
rubrics_metrics.description: When an inventor's improvement of a complicated machine is a small proportion of the whole, if he claims the entire improved machine he should distinctly point out the small addition or alteration which constitutes the improvement; otherwise the claim may be too wide or misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your improvement is minor relative to a known machine, expressly identify and describe that improvement even if you claim the whole machine, to avoid the claim being held vague or concealing the real invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity is fatal; state invention and limits distinctly
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification must state distinctly what the invention is and the limits within which the patentee is to enjoy the monopoly; equivocal or ambiguous claims/descriptions that leave doubt as to what is claimed render the specification bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous phrases ('of any size' etc.) and equivocal wording. Make the scope of the monopoly and the nature of the invention clear so third parties can know what is off-limits (Hastings v. Brown; Turnor v. Winter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not set forth alternative methods if one is ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: If two methods of doing a thing are described and by one of these it cannot be done, the specification is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When providing alternative procedures, confirm each is operative. Do not describe ineffective alternatives even if they might seem obviously inoperative to experts (Medlock's aniline dyes example).

rubrics_metrics.name: No misdirections or misrepresentations in important parts
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification contains language calculated to mislead about an important part (positive misdirections as to mode of operating or materials), or asserts something immaterial which is in reality material, the patent will be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure instructions and material specifications are correct and not misleading. Do not tell the public to perform a wrong action or include impracticable material forms. Courts may invalidate patents where following directions leads to failure (Palmer v. Wagstaff; peroxide example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not materially misrepresent capabilities or objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Misrepresentations as to the object or capabilities of the invention, or other important matters (e.g., claiming a machine will produce a wide range of outputs when it cannot), will deprive the inventor of his patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be accurate about what the invention can do. Overstating capabilities or claiming broader functionality than demonstrated risks patent invalidation (paper-width machine example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible to suggest broader applications if not claiming them
rubrics_metrics.description: Stating that an invention capable of application to other purposes beyond that for which protection is claimed, without describing how those purposes are to be effected, does not necessarily invalidate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to note potential applications beyond the principal embodiment, provided you do not claim exclusive rights over those un-described applications or mislead about them (Cole v. Saqui).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technical and scientific terms with correct meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: In making use of technical language great care should be taken that the words are employed in their true meanings and proper significations; misuse of scientific terms can seriously jeopardize a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise, industry-standard terms. Misuse of terms (e.g., chemical gas names) risks misinterpretation and invalidation, though courts may sometimes adopt a benevolent construction if context clarifies meaning (Edison v. Woodhouse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor lexical mistakes tolerated if meaning clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple mistakes — words used in an inaccurate sense but explained by context or drawings — will not avoid the patent. Courts will overlook minute unimportant errors provided the patentee's meaning is clear to the intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be cavalier about errors, but know that minor slips (translation issues, imprecise words) that do not obscure the invention are usually forgiven. The requirement is intelligibility to the persons addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete specification must end with a distinct claim
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute a complete specification must end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed; 'distinct' contemplates a summary of the main features to which the reader may readily refer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a clear claim section at the end of the specification that summarizes the characteristic features of what is claimed. Although historically judicial opinions differ on the precise breadth of 'distinct', include an explicit, readable claim statement to satisfy the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims operate as disclaimers of unclaimed subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything described in the specification that is not expressly claimed is impliedly disclaimed; the claim defines the boundary of the patentee's monopoly and everything else falls open to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate about what you claim: do not inadvertently give away valuable embodiments by omitting them from the claims. Conversely, avoid claiming beyond what you have described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and breadth of claims carry risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing a large number of claims is a dangerous practice: the more claims, the greater the risks (e.g., many of Edison's numerous claims were later struck out).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance breadth and number of claims strategically. Excessive or poorly drafted multiple claims increase exposure to objection, disclaimers, or invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must show clearly what is intended to be claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be framed so that it can be seen without difficulty what the inventor wishes to secure; ambiguity as to whether a claim is for a combination or for constituent parts can invalidate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims that unambiguously state whether the protection sought is for a combination or for individual parts. If reliance is on a combination claim, ensure the specification enables a competent workman to make the combination without experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims valid when specification enables construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim for a combination will not be deemed too vague when there is proof that a competent workman can make the combination from the specification without experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming combinations, ensure the description enables straightforward construction by skilled artisans. Reference to drawings in conjunction with description can cure initial over-general descriptions (Daw v. Eley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are to ascertain scope, not to teach manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is not intended to aid the description (i.e., to teach how to make the device), but to ascertain the extent of what is claimed as new; if the description is precise, claims may use more general expressions without being fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the specification itself sufficiently precise for enablement; the claims define legal scope. Avoid using the claim as a substitute for a clear technical disclosure, but do not fear using broader terminology in claims where the body furnishes the enabling details.
